traveler: Polybius of Megalopolis, son of Lycortas
title: The Hostage Who Explained Rome: Megalopolis, the Thousand, and the Burning of Carthage
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The House of Lycortas at Megalopolis

stops.name: Megalopolis, born into the federal house
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No ancient text gives a birth year. The standard modern reconstruction works back from his known offices to c. 200 BCE; James Lloyd, writing for the World History Encyclopedia, prefers c. 208 BCE. The two estimates are recorded here unreconciled, and the eight years between them matter later for how far he stood from Hannibal's crossing.
stops.campa: Megalopolis was raised a century before as one wall against Sparta, Arcadian villages gathered inside a single circuit, and it has been federal ground ever since. Into it a son is born to Lycortas, statesman and general of the Achaean League and political heir of Philopoemen. The one standing question in that house is how a small state survives a large one, and the boy grows up among the decrees, treaty drafts and embassies through which the League keeps asking it. He will name himself all his life as Polybius of Megalopolis, son of Lycortas. Other cities will one day cut the same phrase on his behalf into stone.
suggested_refs: The theatre and agora district of ancient Megalopolis, Arcadia
sources: Pausanias, Description of Greece 8.9 and 8.30 (honorific inscriptions naming him son of Lycortas)

stops.name: Megalopolis, the education of a statesman's son
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. No tutor, school or curriculum for Polybius survives. The content is inferred backward from his own list, in Histories 12, of the competencies a serious historian must hold, and from his father's office.
stops.campa: He is taught what a landed Arcadian son is taught: to ride, to hunt, to handle weapons, to bear a camp. He is taught the other half of his father's trade as well, the reading of decrees, treaty clauses and federal correspondence, the archive as a working instrument rather than a store. The standard he will lay down later is formed inside this house: a man who has never held office, never inspected ground and never handled a document is unfit to write history. No tutor's name survives from these years, and no schoolroom.
stops.quote: the soundest education and training for a life of active politics is the study of History
stops.quote_source: Polybius, Histories 1.1.2, Loeb translation (W. R. Paton), Penelope UChicago
suggested_refs: Polybius, Histories Book 12, on the competencies required of a historian
sources: Polybius, Histories 1.1.2 and Book 12, Loeb/Paton via penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Megalopolis, carrying the urn of Philopoemen
stops.date_confidence: attested. Plutarch, Life of Philopoemen 21, and Polybius's own narrative. This is the earliest securely dated event of his life; the month is not given and defaults to January.
stops.campa: The Messenians take Philopoemen alive, hold him below ground and put him to death by poison. The League recovers the body, burns it, and carries the ashes home. It is the first day of Polybius's life that can be given a date. At the head of the procession into Megalopolis he walks, not yet twenty, carrying the urn. The dead man is the last Achaean general who could make Rome negotiate rather than instruct. Behind the urn come the magistrates, the cavalry, and the Messenian prisoners, who are stoned at the tomb.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Philopoemen at Megalopolis

stops.name: Aigion, the seat of the League
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Aigion's role as the Achaean federal capital is attested; no surviving passage places the young Polybius there on any given day. The date orders the segment and nothing more.
stops.campa: The League meets at Aigion above the gulf, where the synod gathers and foreign embassies are received. In that hall a wrong wording can cost a war. Lycortas moves in the room and his son moves behind him, learning the order of business: who may speak, what a decree must contain, how a federal answer to a foreign power is drafted so that it binds every city and not one. The quoted clauses and the counted votes that later fill the Histories are picked up here.
suggested_refs: The federal assembly ground of the Achaean League at Aigion
sources: Polybius, Histories Books 2 and 4, on Achaean federal procedure
F. W. Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius

segments.name: The Cavalry Command and the Year of Pydna

stops.name: Aigion, the offer Rome does not take up
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Achaean offer and for Polybius's readiness to serve, in his own fragmentary account of the debate. The meeting place is inferred from Aigion's role as federal seat and is not stated in the source.
stops.campa: Rome is at war with Perseus of Macedon and the League has to decide what it is. The assembly votes to put its whole force at Rome's disposal, and Polybius is among the men who make ready to march. He writes the debate down later from inside it, one of the few passages in the Histories where the historian is himself in the scene, and what he records is its own answer about what an ally has become. The Roman commanders never call the troops up. The offer is left standing in the air, neither accepted nor declined.
suggested_refs: Polybius, Histories, fragments on the Achaean offer of aid in the Third Macedonian War
sources: Polybius, Histories, fragments on the Achaean offer, summarized in Walbank's commentary

stops.name: Aigion, elected hipparchos of the League
stops.date_confidence: attested that he held the office; the year is the standard reconstruction of 170/169 BCE. James Lloyd, for the World History Encyclopedia, places the hipparchy around 178 BCE instead. The contradiction is not resolved here. The site of the election is not recorded.
stops.campa: He is elected hipparchos, commander of the federal cavalry, the second annual office of the League and normally the step before the generalship his father held. He is about thirty, or about forty if the earlier birth date is right. The cavalry he inherits is in poor condition and he says so; he tours the cities, drills the squadrons, treats the command as an administrative problem rather than an honour. It is the highest place he will ever reach in his own country. Two years later he is on a ship to Italy under guard.
suggested_refs: The annual federal offices of the Achaean League: strategos and hipparchos
sources: Polybius, Histories, on his own hipparchy
F. W. Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius

stops.name: Achaea, the news from Pydna
stops.date_confidence: the battle is attested and dated; Polybius's whereabouts on the day are not recorded anywhere. He is placed in Achaea because his federal office and his deportation the following year both belong to the Peloponnese, and the stop is his receipt of the news, not the battle.
stops.campa: In a Macedonian afternoon the phalanx of Perseus breaks against the legions and the last Antigonid kingdom ends inside an hour. Polybius is in Achaea. The news settles nothing at home and reopens everything: with Macedon gone, no Greek power can balance Rome, and the only remaining question in Achaean politics is which Achaeans backed which side. The man who won the battle is Lucius Aemilius Paullus, in whose house Polybius will be living within a year. Callicrates and the pro-Roman party have waited years for exactly this.
stops.quote: Fortune has guided almost all the affairs of the world in one direction and has forced them to incline towards one and the same end
stops.quote_source: Polybius, Histories 1.4.1, Loeb translation (W. R. Paton), Penelope UChicago
suggested_refs: The battlefield of Pydna in Pieria, Macedonia

stops.name: Achaea, the list of Callicrates
stops.date_confidence: attested. Polybius 30.32 gives the detention of the accused men without trial; the figure of a thousand comes from Pausanias 7.10. The physical site of the selection is not recorded, and the pin is the federal seat as the likeliest venue.
stops.campa: Callicrates hands the Roman commissioners a list of names. About a thousand Achaeans, the men who argued for neutrality and the men who merely hesitated, are taken up and shipped to Italy to answer charges that are never formulated before a court that never sits. Polybius, hipparch the year before, is on it. The case against him is that his house has held federal office for two generations. There is no trial, no sentence, no term set, and no procedure by which any of it could be contested.
stops.quote: the surest and indeed the only method of learning how to bear bravely the vicissitudes of fortune, is to recall the calamities of others
stops.quote_source: Polybius, Histories 1.1.2, Loeb translation (W. R. Paton), Penelope UChicago
suggested_refs: Polybius, Histories 30.32, on the Achaeans held without trial

segments.name: Rome: Seventeen Years Without a Trial

stops.name: Rome, the household of Aemilius Paullus
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was kept at Rome rather than dispersed and that he entered the Paullus circle; the Palatine pin is the conventional location of the family's house and is not fixed by a text.
stops.campa: The detainees are broken up and parcelled out to towns around Italy. Polybius is not. Rank and education buy him Rome itself and a place in the house of Lucius Aemilius Paullus, the general whose victory produced the list he is on. In that house are Paullus's two sons, Quintus Fabius Maximus and the younger boy adopted into the Cornelii Scipiones. The hostage sits at the victor's table. The arrangement gives him the run of the Roman governing class, which no Greek before him has had and no Roman would have granted a free man. He is thirty-three, or forty-one if the earlier birth date is right, and he cannot leave Italy.
suggested_refs: The house of the Aemilii Paulli on the Palatine
sources: Polybius, Histories Book 31, Loeb/Paton via penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Rome, the boy who asks not to be left out
stops.date_confidence: attested at Histories 31.23-24, but the year requires care. Polybius says Scipio was 'not more than eighteen'; Scipio Aemilianus was born in 185 BCE and Polybius reached Rome in 167, which puts the conversation at 167/166, not the c. 161 that some reconstructions give.
stops.campa: Walking back from Fabius's house, the younger brother falls in beside him, colours, and says he is hurt: that Polybius speaks always with his elder brother and never with him, and that he takes this for the family's opinion, that he is the mild one and the least Roman of them. Polybius answers that he addresses the elder first because he is the elder, and that everything he has is at the disposal of them both. The boy takes his hand. He is not more than eighteen. From that day, Polybius writes, he never left his side.
stops.quote: the loan of some books and conversation about them
stops.quote_source: Polybius, Histories 31.23, Loeb translation (W. R. Paton), on how the acquaintance began
suggested_refs: Polybius, Histories 31.23-24, the fullest surviving self-portrait of the historian

stops.name: Rome, the praetor and the single exemption
stops.date_confidence: attested in Histories Book 31 that Fabius and Scipio petitioned the praetor and that the request was granted; the month is not given and the pin is the Forum, where a praetor held court.
stops.campa: When the order comes to send the remaining detainees out to the Italian towns, Fabius and Scipio go to the praetor and ask, as a private favour to their house, that this one Achaean be left in Rome. It is granted. A Roman magistrate makes an exception to a security measure because two boys of a consular family want their friend near them. The other nine hundred and ninety-nine go where they are sent, and most of them die there. Polybius records the intervention plainly. He does not say what it cost him to owe it.
suggested_refs: Polybius, Histories Book 31, on the petition to the praetor
sources: Polybius, Histories Book 31, Loeb/Paton via penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Rome, the library of King Perseus
stops.date_confidence: the disposal of Perseus's library to Paullus's sons is attested at Plutarch, Life of Aemilius Paullus 28. That Polybius read in it is reconstruction, grounded in his residence in that household and in his own account of the books that began the friendship.
stops.campa: Paullus turns the Macedonian treasure over to the public account and keeps nothing out of it, with one exception. The library of King Perseus he allows his sons to choose from for themselves, because they are devoted to learning. The books of a defeated king become working material for the man writing the explanation of the defeat. The Antigonid royal collection arrives on the Palatine as a private inheritance for two boys, and the Achaean living in the house reads in it.
stops.quote: It was only the books of the king that he allowed his sons, who were devoted to learning, to choose out for themselves.
suggested_refs: The royal library of the Antigonids at Pella, carried to Rome after Pydna

stops.name: Rome, the treaties in the Temple of Saturn
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. That he compared documents is attested by his own method statements and by his handling of the Roman treaties with Carthage at Histories 3.26; that the specific texts were consulted in the Temple of Saturn, the state archive and treasury, is a reasonable identification of where such records were kept and is not stated in any ancient source.
stops.campa: Rome keeps its treaties where it keeps its money. A man forbidden to go home is handed the archive of the power holding him: Polybius, through the house he lives in, gets at the records. Method and captivity are one thing here. He later sets out the successive Roman agreements with Carthage clause by clause and argues in detail that the historian Philinus invented one of them. He can make that case only because he has read the bronze and the tablets rather than the books about them.
stops.quote: For just as a living creature which has lost its eyesight is wholly incapacitated, so if History is stripped of her truth all that is left is but an idle tale
stops.quote_source: Polybius, Histories 1.14.5-6, Loeb translation (W. R. Paton), Penelope UChicago
suggested_refs: The Temple of Saturn in the Roman Forum, aerarium and record repository
sources: Polybius, Histories 3.26 (the Philinus treaty) and Book 12 (method), Loeb/Paton via penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Cape Lacinium, the bronze tablet in the temple of Hera
stops.date_confidence: attested that Polybius used the Lacinian bronze inscription as his source for Hannibal's numbers (Histories 3.33 and 3.56) and that he treats it as an inspected document. The year of the visit is unrecorded and is set here inside the Italian detention, when he was in Italy and unable to leave it.
stops.campa: On the promontory below Croton, in the sanctuary of Hera Lacinia, Hannibal set up a bronze plate before he left Italy, listing his marches, his musters and his losses in Punic and in Greek. Polybius trusts bronze over rumour, which means travelling to the bronze. He goes to the temple and reads it. Every figure he gives for the size of the Carthaginian army in Italy rests on that plate, and he says so, setting a document the general commissioned against the numbers other writers pass around.
suggested_refs: The temple of Hera Lacinia at Capo Colonna, Calabria, and Hannibal's bilingual inscription
sources: Polybius, Histories 3.33 and 3.56, Loeb/Paton via penelope.uchicago.edu
working/journeys/hannibal.journey.json, stop 'Cape Lacinium, the bronze tablet in Hera's temple'

stops.name: Lilybaeum, the ground of the first war
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Polybius's long First Punic War narrative in Book 1 and his programmatic insistence on personal inspection make Sicilian research probable; no surviving passage places him at Lilybaeum, and Sicily was a province rather than one of the Italian towns the detainees were assigned to.
stops.campa: The first war between Rome and Carthage is sixty years finished when he writes it, and he writes it at length: twenty-three years of fighting over this island, fleets built and sunk and built again, sieges at the western end. Lilybaeum is the hinge, held by Carthage against every Roman attempt until the peace treaty gave it away. His own rule is that a man who has not seen ground should not describe ground, and the coast he describes is described exactly. No text puts him on the mole or inside the walls. Whether he ever crossed to Sicily at all is not recorded.
suggested_refs: The Punic defences of Lilybaeum, modern Marsala
sources: Polybius, Histories Book 1 (First Punic War) and Book 12 (autopsy), Loeb/Paton via penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Rome, five tablets and twenty-five letters
stops.date_confidence: the passage is attested at Histories 10.45-47 (chapters 43-44 cover the older and cruder fire-signals he is superseding). When and where he composed it is not recorded; the date only places it inside the Roman years.
stops.campa: He sets down a way to send any message whatever over a distance by fire. Divide the alphabet into five groups of five and give each party five tablets; torches raised on the left name the group, torches on the right the letter within it, and a pair of sighting tubes fixes the two points of light so they cannot be confused. He credits the scheme to Cleoxenus and Democleitus and claims for himself only its perfection, a sentence the manuals that call the grid by his name alone leave out. Anything that can be spelled can be sent.
stops.quote: We take the alphabet and divide it into five parts, each consisting of five letters
stops.quote_source: Polybius, Histories 10.45.6-7, Loeb translation (W. R. Paton), Penelope UChicago
suggested_refs: Polybius, Histories 10.45-47, on the dioptra and the alphabetic fire-signal

stops.name: Rome, the Forum, the embassies that are shelved
stops.date_confidence: attested that Achaean embassies petitioned repeatedly across the detention years and that many detainees died before any decision; no single year is fixed, and the date given stands for a process running from 167 to 150.
stops.campa: Year after year the Achaeans send embassies to the Senate asking that the detained men be tried or released, and year after year the Senate declines to take the question up. Polybius watches the procedure from inside the city and writes, of the constitution that is doing this to him, that consuls, Senate and people so hamper and assist one another that no better political system can be found. Both judgements stand in the same set of books. The men grow old in the Italian towns and start to die there.
stops.quote: Such being the power that each part has of hampering the others or co-operating with them, their union is adequate to all emergencies, so that it is impossible to find a better political system than this
stops.quote_source: Polybius, Histories 6.18.1, Loeb translation (W. R. Paton), Penelope UChicago
suggested_refs: The Curia Hostilia and the Comitium, where the Senate heard foreign embassies

stops.name: Rome, Cato ends the debate
stops.date_confidence: attested in Plutarch, Life of Cato the Elder 9, which names Polybius directly both in the release and in the later petition. Plutarch is writing some two and a half centuries after the scene; the wording of Cato's two jokes is his.
stops.campa: The question comes back to the Senate and Cato closes it. He says he has nothing better to do than sit all day debating whether a few old Greeks are to be carried to their graves by Italian undertakers or by their own. The survivors, some three hundred of the thousand, are released. Polybius comes back the same day to ask that the freed men be restored to their honours at home, and Cato laughs at him: a man who has got out of the Cyclops's cave and is going back in for the cap and belt he left behind.
suggested_refs: Plutarch, Life of Cato the Elder 9, the two exchanges with Polybius
sources: Plutarch, Life of Cato the Elder 9 (Perseus/LacusCurtius)

segments.name: Released, and the Burning of Carthage

stops.name: Megalopolis, home after seventeen years
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was released in 150 BCE and returned; the month is not recorded and defaults here to summer only as an ordering device.
stops.campa: He goes home. Seventeen years in Italy, no charge, no hearing, no verdict, and Arcadia at the end of it. He is about fifty. The father whose career put him on the list is dead. The League he was hipparch of is now in the hands of men who will take it to war with Rome inside four years. He has spent the detention becoming the only Greek alive who can explain the Roman state to Greeks and the Greek world to Romans. Neither side has asked him for the explanation. He does not stay long. The house at Megalopolis is standing.
suggested_refs: Megalopolis in the last years of the independent Achaean League
sources: F. W. Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius

stops.name: Rome, attached to Scipio for the African war
stops.date_confidence: attested that he was with Scipio in Africa (Histories Book 38 fragment: 'Polybius the Achaean, though he was then with Scipio in Africa'). His legal or military capacity is nowhere defined; no title survives, and the Rome pin marks the departure rather than a documented scene.
stops.campa: Rome declares war on Carthage and Scipio Aemilianus goes to Africa. Polybius, released and free to be anywhere in the world, attaches himself to him. No source gives him a rank, a command or a salary. He is present, he is consulted, he is sent on the sort of errand a staff officer is sent on. The friendship formed in a hostage's first Roman winter has turned into the working arrangement of a fifty-year-old historian and the man who will finish the third and last war between the two cities. He goes because Scipio asks.
suggested_refs: Polybius, Histories Book 38, on his presence with Scipio in Africa
sources: Polybius, Histories Book 38 fragment, Loeb/Paton via penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Cirta, sent to Masinissa for elephants
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. A fragment records a naval mission connected with obtaining elephants from Masinissa; the outcome is lost, and Cirta is given as the Numidian royal seat rather than as an attested endpoint of the journey.
stops.campa: Masinissa, king of the Numidians, is nearly ninety and dying, and the Roman army in Africa wants his elephants. Scipio sends Polybius by sea on the business. The fragment shows the shape of his position in these years: a Greek holding no office at all, carrying a Roman general's request to an African king, and afterwards writing the one account of the war that all three parties would have recognised as the war. Whether he reached Cirta, whether he saw the old king, whether he came back with anything, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: The Numidian royal seat at Cirta under Masinissa
sources: Polybius, Histories, fragment on the Masinissa mission, flagged as fragmentary in Walbank's commentary

stops.name: Utica, the base of the siege
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Utica's role as the Roman headquarters is documented; Polybius's presence there specifically is not stated in any surviving passage, only his presence in the theatre of war.
stops.campa: Utica went over to Rome before the fighting started and pays for it with its harbour: the army lands here, the fleet lies here, the siege of Carthage is run from here. Twenty miles down the coast the city is being killed. No text names Polybius in Utica. Every text that puts him in Africa at all puts him where the Roman camp is, and for three years the Roman camp is this one. It is where a man attached to the staff would pass those years, riding out to the lines and back.
suggested_refs: Utica, Roman headquarters in the Third Punic War and later provincial capital
sources: Standard accounts of Utica's role in the Third Punic War

stops.name: Carthage, the Byrsa hill as the city burns
stops.date_confidence: attested that Polybius was present at the destruction. The weeping and the Homeric line come through Appian, Punic Wars 132, which states that Polybius wrote it down as he heard it; Polybius's own Book 38 survives only in fragments, so the scene reaches us through a later quoter and some scholars read it as literary shaping.
stops.campa: The city has been burning for days. On the height of the Byrsa, with the last quarter falling, Scipio stands looking at it and weeps for his enemy, and speaks the lines of Homer about the day when sacred Troy shall perish and Priam with his people. Polybius, who has been at his side for thirty years, asks him what he means by it. Scipio takes his hand and names his own country, saying he fears the same for Rome when he considers how human things turn over. Polybius writes it down as he heard it.
stops.quote: A glorious moment, Polybius; but I have a dread foreboding that some day the same doom will be pronounced on my own country
stops.quote_source: Polybius, Histories 38.21, Loeb translation (W. R. Paton), Penelope UChicago
suggested_refs: The Byrsa hill at Carthage, and Appian, Punic Wars 132, which preserves the scene from Polybius

stops.name: Carthage, the news that Achaea has gone to war
stops.date_confidence: attested in Histories Book 38 that he learned of the Achaean disaster while with Scipio in Africa; the month is not recorded and is set after the fall of Carthage in spring 146 to keep the order.
stops.campa: While Africa burns, the Achaean League has gone to war with Rome under Critolaus and Diaeus, and word of it reaches the camp. Polybius is in the ruins of one city hearing that his own country has picked the same fight. He writes afterwards that though he was then with Scipio in Africa he could not be indifferent to the disaster at home. He was in a position to know what the alternative had been. On the men who caused it he uses the plainest words he has. He writes nothing in their defence.
suggested_refs: Polybius, Histories Book 38, on the Achaean War and its leaders
sources: Polybius, Histories Book 38, Loeb/Paton via penelope.uchicago.edu

segments.name: The Settlement of a Defeated Country

stops.name: Corinth, arriving at the site of a city
stops.date_confidence: the destruction of Corinth by Lucius Mummius in 146 BCE is attested across the ancient tradition. Polybius was in Africa when it happened; the date and circumstances of his arrival afterwards are not recorded, and the autumn date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Mummius takes Corinth, kills the men, sells the women and children, ships the statues to Italy and destroys what is left. The League that Polybius held office in stops existing inside a week. He is in Africa when it happens, and comes back to a site rather than a city. For twenty years he had argued that Greek politicians who provoke Rome do not understand what they are provoking, and the proof has been supplied by his own country at its own expense. The Histories will have to run four years past the ending he designed for them. Corinth and Carthage fall in the same year.
suggested_refs: The destruction layer of 146 BCE at ancient Corinth
sources: Pausanias and Strabo on the destruction of Corinth

stops.name: The Achaean cities, framing the new constitutions
stops.date_confidence: reported by Pausanias and consistently repeated in the secondary literature on Polybius; the exact chapter was not re-verified against the primary text in this pass, and the scale of his authority is a tradition rather than a documented commission.
stops.campa: Rome hands him the settlement. He goes through the Peloponnese city by city arranging constitutions, boundaries and debts, a defeated man given authority by the victors over his own defeated country. Pausanias reports that the cities set up statues to him afterwards, and that the verses cut under one of them said he had roamed over every land and sea, had been the ally of the Romans, and had stayed their anger against the Greeks. Whether the anger was really stayed by him is not a thing the record can settle.
suggested_refs: Pausanias, Description of Greece, on the honorific relief and verses for Polybius at Megalopolis

stops.name: Olympia, a base said to carry his name
stops.date_confidence: unverified tradition. A statue base at Olympia honouring Polybius as a Megalopolitan is reported in the background material and was not independently located in a primary or secondary source during this pass. The date is postwar by inference only.
stops.campa: At Olympia, among the bases carrying the names of victors, generals and kings, a stone is said to have carried his: Polybius of Megalopolis. The sanctuary is where the Greek world keeps its memory of itself in bronze and in rows, under a peace that only ever held for the festival. A base there for a historian who spent seventeen years as a Roman detainee and came home to write the explanation of Greek subjection would be worth having. It is worth recording as a tradition. The stone has not been produced.
suggested_refs: The statue bases of the Altis at Olympia
sources: Reported as an epigraphic tradition in the background dossier; not independently confirmed in this pass

stops.name: Kleitor, the armed man in the relief
stops.date_confidence: the relief is Hellenistic and was excavated at Kleitor in 1880, published by L. Gurlitt in 1881, who proposed the identification. No inscription on it names Polybius. The date given is an ordering device inside his lifetime and carries no claim that the piece was carved then or that he sat for it.
stops.campa: At Kleitor in northern Arcadia a relief comes out of the ground in 1880 showing a man in armour, and its publisher argues the next year that the figure is Polybius. Nothing cut into the stone says so. It is Hellenistic, it is Arcadian, it shows a soldier, and past that the identification rests on a nineteenth-century archaeologist's wish to have a face for the historian. It is the closest thing to a portrait that exists. Nobody knows what he looked like.
suggested_refs: L. Gurlitt, 'Ein Kriegerrelief aus Kleitor,' Mitteilungen des Deutschen Archaologischen Instituts, Athenische Abteilung 6 (1881), 154-166, pl. V
sources: Wikimedia Commons file description for 'Relief aus Kleitor.JPG', citing Gurlitt 1881

segments.name: Going to Look: Other Men's Ground

stops.name: The Rhone crossing, measuring what Hannibal did
stops.date_confidence: attested at Histories 3.42-48 that he undertook the inspection himself; the year is nowhere given, and it is placed after 150 because the detention confined him to Italy. Ancient river toponyms do not map exactly onto the modern stretch, so the coordinates are a reconstruction.
stops.campa: He walks the river. Hannibal brought elephants across it in 218, a decade or two before Polybius was born, and the accounts in circulation have gods appearing to the army and mountains no man could climb. Polybius goes to the bank, looks at the width and the current, works out where a force with animals could get over, and questions the people who live there. No gods appear anywhere in what he writes. What comes of it reads like a survey: distances in stades, days of march, the state of the crops on the far side.
stops.quote: After a ten days' march of eight hundred stades along the bank of the Isere Hannibal began the ascent of the Alps and now found himself involved in very great difficulties
stops.quote_source: Polybius, Histories 3.50.1-2, Loeb translation (W. R. Paton), Penelope UChicago
suggested_refs: Polybius, Histories 3.42-48, the Rhone crossing

stops.name: Col de la Traversette, the pass still argued over
stops.date_confidence: attested that he examined the Alpine terrain himself (Histories 3.48-56). Which pass his description matches is contested modern scholarship, not an ancient statement: the Traversette is one candidate among several and F. W. Walbank rejected it. The pin is therefore a scholarly hypothesis, not an attested location.
stops.campa: He climbs. He states in the book that he questioned men who had been there and looked at the ground himself, and he states it because the alternative on offer is writers who make the Alps impassable in order to make the crossing miraculous. The dispute exists at all because he wrote precisely enough to be checked against rock two thousand years later. The Traversette is one candidate; Walbank, his principal modern commentator, threw it out. Which pass he is describing is argued to this day.
stops.quote: Of course Hannibal did not act as these writers describe, but conducted his plans with sound practical sense. He had ascertained by careful inquiry the richness of the country
stops.quote_source: Polybius, Histories 3.48.10-11, Loeb translation (W. R. Paton), Penelope UChicago
suggested_refs: The competing candidate passes for Hannibal's crossing: Traversette, Clapier, Col du Mont Cenis
sources: F. W. Walbank, A Historical Commentary on Polybius

stops.name: The Pillars of Heracles, out through the strait
stops.date_confidence: tradition, and thin. Pliny the Elder associates Polybius with an Atlantic coastal voyage said to have been provided for by Scipio, and reproduces an itinerary; the extent and the route are disputed, and Book 34, where Polybius would have given his own account, survives only in fragments. Not independently verified in this pass.
stops.campa: Beyond the strait the Mediterranean ends and the ocean starts, and Roman knowledge of the African shore south of it is rumour with a Carthaginian lock on it, a lock that came off in 146. Pliny, writing two centuries later, says Polybius went through and coasted down in a squadron Scipio gave him, and reproduces an itinerary of rivers and headlands. The voyage rests on that Roman encyclopaedist's say-so and on nothing else. Book 34, where Polybius would have told it in his own words, is gone.
suggested_refs: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, on the Polybian Atlantic itinerary
sources: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, as cited in secondary treatments of Polybius's lost Book 34; tradition, not independently verified here

stops.name: Gades, the port at the edge of the ocean
stops.date_confidence: geographic inference. Gades is the standard ancient departure point for Atlantic voyages along Africa, which makes it the plausible staging point for the disputed reconnaissance; no ancient text places Polybius there by name.
stops.campa: Gades is the old Phoenician town at the world's edge, the port every Atlantic voyage in antiquity leaves from, and where a squadron going down the African coast would take on water. No text puts Polybius on this quay. Of every traveller's tale he asks the question a treasury asks: his standing objection to Pytheas of Massalia is not that the northern voyage was impossible but that a private man of small means could never have paid for one. Who paid for his own passage down the African coast, if he ever made it, is not recorded either.
stops.quote: Pytheas says that he personally visited the whole northern coast of Europe as far as the ends of the world, a thing we would not even believe of Hermes himself if he told us so
stops.quote_source: Polybius, Histories 34.5.9, preserved via Strabo, Loeb translation (W. R. Paton), Penelope UChicago
suggested_refs: Gades (Cadiz) as the ancient staging point for Atlantic navigation
sources: Polybius, Histories 34.5, preserved in Strabo, Geography 2.4, Loeb/Paton via penelope.uchicago.edu

segments.name: Book Thirty-Four, and the Last Roads

stops.name: Rome, who paid for Pytheas
stops.date_confidence: attested that Polybius attacked Pytheas in Book 34; the polemic survives only through Strabo's quotation at Geography 2.4, so the wording reaches us at one remove. The date and the Roman setting are conventional placings of his late geographical work, not fixed by any text.
stops.campa: Book 34 is his geography, and in it he goes after Pytheas of Massalia, dead a century and a half, who claimed to have walked round the whole of Britain, gave the island a circumference of forty thousand stades, put an island called Thule six days further out, and described a sea-lung that was neither land nor water nor air. The objection is unanswerable, and it is not the same thing as a refutation. Polybius answers with the accounts: a poor private citizen could not have travelled from Cadiz to the Don.
stops.quote: Pytheas who has led many people into error by saying that he traversed the whole of Britain on foot, giving the island a circumference of forty thousand stades
stops.quote_source: Polybius, Histories 34.5.2, preserved via Strabo, Loeb translation (W. R. Paton), Penelope UChicago
suggested_refs: Strabo, Geography 2.4, which preserves the whole of Polybius's case against Pytheas
sources: Polybius, Histories 34.5, via Strabo, Geography 2.4, Loeb/Paton on penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Numantia, the last campaign he is placed at
stops.date_confidence: tradition. Modern scholarship treats his presence at Numantia as probable and the details as much less secure than for Carthage; no surviving Polybian passage confirmed in this pass places him at the siege. The lost monograph on the Numantine War is likewise reported rather than verified.
stops.campa: Scipio is sent to Spain to finish a war Rome has been losing for twenty years, and takes the Celtiberian town by starving it out. The survivors kill themselves or are sold. Polybius is generally said to have been there and to have written a book about the siege afterwards. The book is lost and no surviving line of his own puts him on that hillside. He is past seventy, and everything about his presence comes from later report rather than from him.
suggested_refs: The Roman circumvallation of Numantia, excavated by Adolf Schulten
sources: Tradition reported in modern Polybian scholarship; not independently confirmed in this pass

stops.name: Narbo, a new road entered in the book
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction resting on a fragment. A passage connected with Polybius mentions the Via Domitia, conventionally dated to the Roman campaigns of 121-118 BCE. If the fragment is genuinely his and the dating holds, it is the latest marker of his writing life; neither the attribution nor the date was independently re-verified here.
stops.campa: A fragment attached to his name mentions the road the Romans are driving through Transalpine Gaul, the Via Domitia, laid out in the years after 121. If the fragment is his and the dating holds he is over eighty and still adding to the work: a new road in a new province, entered into a history that was meant to close at 168 and then closed again at 146. The last dated thing in his writing life is a piece of infrastructure, which is the kind of fact he preferred. Whether the fragment is his at all has never been settled.
suggested_refs: The Via Domitia through Narbo Martius, Rome's first road in Transalpine Gaul
sources: Fragment discussion reported via Wikipedia, 'Polybius'; not independently verified in this pass

stops.name: Megalopolis, thrown from the horse on the farm road
stops.date_confidence: tradition, from a single late source. Pseudo-Lucian, Macrobii 22, a Roman-period compilation, says he fell from his horse riding home from his farm, sickened and died at eighty-two. There is no contemporary corroboration, no inscription, and no grave. The year 118 comes from subtracting eighty-two from a birth date that is itself a reconstruction.
stops.campa: He is riding back from his farm to the town when the horse throws him. He takes to his bed with the injury and dies of it at eighty-two, according to a Roman-period compiler of the lives of long-lived men, who gives him his full formal name: Polybius, son of Lycortas, of Megalopolis. The year is arrived at by arithmetic on two uncertain numbers. No tomb, no epitaph and no grave has ever been found. That single sentence is the entire record of his death.
suggested_refs: Pseudo-Lucian, Macrobii 22, the only ancient notice of Polybius's death
sources: Pseudo-Lucian, Macrobii 22, as cited by Wikipedia, 'Polybius'

stops.name: Constantinople, the historians cut into files
stops.date_confidence: attested as standard textual-transmission scholarship. The Excerpta Constantiniana were compiled in the tenth century under Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos; the exact year of the Polybian extracts is not fixed and 950 stands for the reign. Posthumous by a thousand years: the text travels here, not the man.
stops.campa: Forty books existed. Five come through whole, the sixth nearly so, and the rest would have gone entirely if a tenth-century emperor had not set scholars to cutting the Greek historians into topical volumes: On Embassies, On Virtues and Vices, On Plots. Polybius is quarried for these files. They save him by dismembering him: what the excerptors took is all that remains of Books 7 to 39, in pieces, out of order, with the narrative that held them together discarded as the part nobody needed.
suggested_refs: The Excerpta Constantiniana, compiled under Constantine VII Porphyrogennetos
sources: Standard classical-scholarship consensus on the Excerpta Constantiniana

stops.name: Rome, five hundred ducats for a Latin Polybius
stops.date_confidence: attested that Niccolo Perotti translated Polybius into Latin for Pope Nicholas V and was paid five hundred ducats. No exact year and no specification of which books; the date is inferred from the pontificate, 1447-1455, and is approximate.
stops.campa: Pope Nicholas V, buying Greek manuscripts and commissioning Latin versions for the library he is founding, pays Niccolo Perotti five hundred ducats to turn Polybius into Latin. The Latin West has had no access to him for centuries. The Renaissance meets the analysis of the Roman constitution as a paid commission, drawn up in the city its author was brought to under guard. Perotti's version circulates in manuscript for decades before anyone prints a line of the Greek.
suggested_refs: Niccolo Perotti's Latin Polybius, commissioned by Nicholas V for the Vatican Library

stops.name: Hagenau, the Greek printed for the first time
stops.date_confidence: attested. The editio princeps of the Historiae was printed at Hagenau in Alsace by Johannes Secerius, edited by Vincentius Obsopoeus, containing Books 1-5 of the Greek with Perotti's Latin.
stops.campa: The Greek text is printed for the first time at Hagenau in Alsace, by Johannes Secerius, edited by Vincentius Obsopoeus: Books 1 to 5, bound together with Perotti's Latin. Those five are also the only five that survive complete, so the volume is, by accident of what the Byzantines kept, nearly the whole of the intact Polybius. Everything said about him in the West for eighty years had come through a translator's choices. From 1530 a reader in Germany or France can have the sentences themselves.
suggested_refs: The 1530 Hagenau editio princeps of Polybius, Books I-V

stops.name: London, Casaubon's four years and the commentary he did not finish
stops.date_confidence: attested with a correction. Wikipedia's bare statement that Casaubon 'left the Polybius unfinished' is misleading: the Dictionary of National Biography records that the work cost him more than four years, that he lived to finish the translation, and that only a fragment of the commentary was published after his death in 1614. His Latin version was carried in the Gronovius (1670) and Ernesti (1763) editions.
stops.campa: Isaac Casaubon spends more than four years on Polybius and brings out the edition with his own Latin translation. The commentary meant to go with it is not finished when he dies in 1614, and a fragment of it is printed afterwards. The unfinished project of a dead scholar becomes the standard Latin Polybius: his translation is carried in the Gronovius edition of 1670 and still in the Ernesti of 1763, a century and a half after he stopped work on it.
suggested_refs: Casaubon's Polybius, 1609, and the posthumous fragment of his commentary
sources: Internet Archive holdings of the Gronovius 1670 and Ernesti 1763 editions

stops.name: London, Dryden writes the preface
stops.date_confidence: attested that Sir Henry Sheeres's English translation of the Histories carried a preface by John Dryden, published 1693.
stops.campa: Sir Henry Sheeres puts the Histories into English and John Dryden writes the preface for it. Polybius enters the language five years after the English have changed kings by agreement and are arguing over which part of the constitution holds which power, with Book 6 in his luggage: consuls, Senate and people, each able to obstruct the others and none able to rule alone. The Poet Laureate performs the introduction. What the book is doing in that argument, the preface does not quite say.
suggested_refs: Sir Henry Sheeres, The History of Polybius (1693), with John Dryden's preface

stops.name: Philadelphia, cited by name in the sixty-third Federalist
stops.date_confidence: attested that James Madison cites Polybius by name in Federalist No. 63. That the framers' checks-and-balances reasoning derives substantially from Book 6 is argued by some modern scholars and disputed by others; it is not settled, and is not asserted here as settled.
stops.campa: Madison cites him by name in the sixty-third Federalist, arguing for the new constitution. The theory in Book 6, that a state endures by mixing monarchy, aristocracy and democracy so that each can check the others, and that unmixed constitutions rot in a fixed order, is in the water the framers are drinking. A book written to explain to Greeks why they lost is put to work laying out a republic. How much of the machinery comes from Polybius and how much from Montesquieu and from English practice is argued over still.
stops.quote: Such is the cycle of political revolution, the course appointed by nature in which constitutions change, disappear, and finally return to the point from which they started
stops.quote_source: Polybius, Histories 6.9.10, Loeb translation (W. R. Paton), Penelope UChicago
suggested_refs: The Federalist No. 63 (Madison), and Polybius, Histories Book 6 on anakyklosis

stops.name: London and Cambridge, the text everyone now reads
stops.date_confidence: attested. W. R. Paton's Greek-English Polybius appeared in six Loeb volumes between 1922 and 1927 (Heinemann, London, and Harvard University Press). The Ortega y Gasset quotation is attested but its exact year is not: it comes from Meditations on Hunting, whose prologue dates to 1942-43.
stops.campa: W. R. Paton's Greek and English Polybius comes out in six Loeb volumes between 1922 and 1927, Heinemann in London and Harvard in Cambridge, and becomes the working text: the one quoted in footnotes, the one keyed into the digital editions, the one through which very nearly everybody now reads him. He is consulted for the constitution, for Hannibal, for the fall of Carthage, and occasionally for himself. The whole of the translation now sits on the open web at a site maintained by one man.
stops.quote: one of the few great minds that the turbid human species has managed to produce
stops.quote_source: Jose Ortega y Gasset, Meditations on Hunting, on Polybius
suggested_refs: The Loeb Polybius, trans. W. R. Paton, 6 vols., 1922-1927
Bill Thayer's LacusCurtius edition at penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Portland, the arcade cabinet that never existed
stops.date_confidence: the legend is documented; the events are not, and there is no evidence any such machine existed. The earliest traceable online source is a coinop.org posting of 1998 whose own stated date appears fabricated, and the first print mention is in GamePro, September 2003. The 1981 date is the claim internal to the legend.
stops.campa: In 1981, the story goes, a black cabinet with no manufacturer's name appears in arcades here, gives the players seizures, nightmares and amnesia, and is carried out at night by men in dark suits who take only the recorded data. No such machine existed. The tale is first traceable to a web posting of 1998, the date on the posting itself apparently invented, and reaches print in 2003. The name it borrowed belongs to a man who held that a history without truth in it is a living creature with its eyes put out.
suggested_refs: Wikipedia, 'Polybius (urban legend)'
sources: Polybius, Histories 1.14.5-6, for the closing image
